retrieved.embedding_text:
Getting repairs done on a rental property > Steps to get urgent repairs done
1

Tell them – in writing if possible – about what needs fixing.

2

Follow up any conversations in writing.

3

Keep a copy of any correspondence or conversations as evidence.

4

If your landlord or agent cannot be contacted or is unwilling or taking too long to arrange repairs, check whether your lease includes details of a preferred tradesperson.

5

Get the repair work done by a licensed tradesperson, preferably one that has been recommended on your lease.

Your landlord or agent may not have to reimburse you for the cost of the repair if:

*   you [caused the damage](https://www.nsw.gov.au/housing-and-construction/rules/fair-wear-and-tear-versus-damage-rental-properties "Fair wear and tear versus damage in rental properties")
*   you didn’t try to contact them about the repair
*   you didn’t give them a reasonable amount of time to organise the repair
*   the repair was not carried out by a licensed tradesperson.

6

Make sure you send written details of repairs, including receipts for the costs, so you can get repaid.

7

You can get repaid for the cost of the work up to $1,000.Your landlord or agent must pay you back within 14 days of your notice.

section_path: What if things go wrong?
retrieved.embedding_text:
Getting repairs done on a rental property > What if things go wrong?
If urgent repairs are not done:

*   do not stop paying the rent. If you [stop paying your rent](https://www.nsw.gov.au/housing-and-construction/rules/non-payment-of-rent "Non-payment of rent"), you will be in breach of your lease agreement, and you could be asked to move out.

For urgent repairs, you need to show that:

*   the problem needing repair was not your fault
*   you made a ‘reasonable’ attempt to contact the landlord/agent
*   you allowed the landlord or agent a ‘reasonable’ chance to do the repairs
*   a repair person named in your tenancy agreement (if possible) or a licensed or qualified tradesperson did the repairs
*   you have copies of all receipts and records of conversations or letters that you have written.

You will need to have your landlord or agent's agreement if any non-urgent repairs are needed and [follow the steps outlined above](https://www.nsw.gov.au/housing-and-construction/renting-a-place-to-live/getting-repairs-done#non-urgent-repairs)to get them done.

If a repair issue is not able to be resolved, you can [lodge a complaint to NSW Fair Trading](https://www.nsw.gov.au/housing-and-construction/renting-a-place-to-live/residential-tenancy-complaints "Residential tenancy complaints") to get help. If the landlord or agent doesn't want to carry out the repairs, NSW Fair Trading may decide to issue a [rectification order](https://www.nsw.gov.au/housing-and-construction/rules/rectification-orders-for-rental-properties "Rectification orders for rental properties").

If this still does not solve the issue, you can escalate the [dispute to the Tribunal](https://www.nsw.gov.au/housing-and-construction/renting-a-place-to-live/residential-rental-bonds/dealing-bond-disputes-for-tenants#toc-going-to-the-tribunal)(NSW Civil and Administrative Tribunal (NCAT)).

To get help and support, go to the [Tenants’ Union of NSW](https://www.tenants.org.au/ "Tenants' Union of New South Wales (https://www.tenants.org.au/)") for legal advice, assistance, and information to tenants, with resources in community languages available. The[NSW Aboriginal Tenancy Advice and Advocacy Services](https://nswats.com.au/how-we-help/) also offers assistance and support for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander tenants.

Request advice before a Tribunal hearing

Do you have a date for a hearing in the NSW Civil and Administrative Tribunal (NCAT)? Get advice from your local Tenants Advice and Advocacy Service.

[Use the Tenants' Union request form](https://www.tenants.org.au/ncatadvice).

[](https://www.nsw.gov.au/housing-and-construction/renting-a-place-to-live/getting-repairs-done)Non-urgent repairs are those that do not need fixing right away. retrieved.embedding_text:
Getting repairs done on a rental property > How do I request a repair be made?
There are two types of repairs: [urgent repairs](https://www.nsw.gov.au/housing-and-construction/renting-a-place-to-live/getting-repairs-done#urgent-repairs) and [non-urgent repairs](https://www.nsw.gov.au/housing-and-construction/renting-a-place-to-live/getting-repairs-done#non-urgent-repairs).

In both circumstances you should contact your landlord or real estate agent first.

If you require urgent repairs and you can't contact your landlord or agent, then you can contact a repair person yourself - see your [residential tenancy agreement](https://www.nsw.gov.au/housing-and-construction/rules/residential-tenancy-agreements "Residential tenancy agreements") for approved or preferred tradespeople to use - and have the costs reimbursed up to $1,000.

![Image 1: Hands holding wrench attached to plumbing pipes under sink.](https://www.nsw.gov.au/sites/default/files/styles/_medium/public/2023-10/GettyImages-1150199946.jpg?itok=lDlK5NvB)

Resolving residential tenancy disputes > Key information
*   The first step in resolving any problem or complaint is to carefully read the terms of your [residential tenancy agreement](https://www.nsw.gov.au/housing-and-construction/rules/residential-tenancy-agreements "Residential tenancy agreements").
*   It is best for the tenant and landlord or agent to try to resolve any issues between themselves.
*   To help reduce further disputes and keep records and evidence if needed, tenants should make requests in writing, including the details of any agreement reached.
*   If an agreement can’t be reached, tenants, landlords and agents have several [options to resolve a dispute](https://www.nsw.gov.au/housing-and-construction/renting-a-place-to-live/resolving-residential-tenancy-disputes#getting-help-with-disputes).

section_path: Resolving disputes through the Tribunal
retrieved.embedding_text:
Resolving residential tenancy disputes > Resolving disputes through the Tribunal
The Tribunal is an independent body that hears and decides on applications for orders from tenants and landlords.

A landlord or tenant can apply directly to the Tribunal for orders relating to a residential tenancy instead of first [making a complaint to Fair Trading](https://www.nsw.gov.au/housing-and-construction/renting-a-place-to-live/residential-tenancy-complaints "Tenancy complaints"), if they wish.

A landlord or tenant can decide to lodge an application with the Tribunal if:

*   Fair Trading cannot find a solution mutually agreed to by both parties.
*   A termination order is being sought.
*   The complaint relates to a matter for which Fair Trading is not able to offer dispute resolution, such as a dispute relating to claiming a bond.

retrieved.embedding_text:
Getting your bond back at the end of a tenancy > Getting your bond back at the end of a tenancy > What if things go wrong?
Things may go wrong if

*   you have not addressed all the things you need to do when ending a tenancy
*   you have a disagreement with your landlord or agent and need to negotiate
*   your [landlord or agent disputes your claim](https://www.nsw.gov.au/housing-and-construction/renting-a-place-to-live/residential-rental-bonds/dealing-bond-disputes-for-tenants "Dealing with bond disputes for tenants")
*   you cannot afford to pay for [damages beyond fair wear and tear](https://www.nsw.gov.au/housing-and-construction/rules/fair-wear-and-tear-versus-damage-rental-properties "Fair wear and tear versus damage in rental properties").

If the issue is not able to be resolved, you or your landlord or agent may need to[take the dispute to the NSW Civil and Administrative Tribunal (NCAT)](https://ncat.nsw.gov.au/case-types/housing-and-property.html "NSW Civil and Administrative Tribunal (https://ncat.nsw.gov.au/case-types/housing-and-property.html)"). This means that the dispute is out of Fair Trading NSW's hands.

To get help, go to the [Tenants’ Union of NSW](https://www.tenants.org.au/ "Tenants' Union of New South Wales (https://www.tenants.org.au/)") for legal advice, assistance, and information to tenants. The Tribunal also provides a useful [list of links to legal help and advice services](https://ncat.nsw.gov.au/help-and-support/get-legal-help-and-advice.html).

If your tenancy is over, you can claim the bond back online

You don’t need to wait for the landlord to release the bond. If you originally submitted your bond online and you have addressed all the things you need to do after ending the tenancy, you can claim the bond on Rental Bonds Online.

[Claim the bond online](https://rbo.fairtrading.nsw.gov.au/tenant/login "Rental Bonds Online registered tenant login (https://rbo.fairtrading.nsw.gov.au/tenant/login)")

Make a complaint to NSW Fair Trading about a bond claim without evidence

If your agent or landlord makes a claim against the bond and does not provide you with evidence of the claim, this is a breach of the Residential Tenancies Act 2010. You should lodge a complaint with NSW Fair Trading to assess their conduct.

[Lodge a complaint with Fair Trading](https://www.nsw.gov.au/housing-and-construction/renting-a-place-to-live/residential-tenancy-complaints "Residential tenancy complaints").

Request advice before a Tribunal hearing

Do you have a date for a hearing in the NSW Civil and Administrative Tribunal (NCAT)? Get advice from your local Tenants Advice and Advocacy Service.

[Use the Tenants' Union request form](https://www.tenants.org.au/ncatadvice)

*   your [landlord or agent disputes your claim](https://www.nsw.gov.au/housing-and-construction/renting-a-place-to-live/residential-rental-bonds/dealing-bond-disputes-for-tenants "Dealing with bond disputes for tenants")
*   you cannot afford to pay for [damages beyond fair wear and tear](https://www.nsw.gov.au/housing-and-construction/rules/fair-wear-and-tear-versus-damage-rental-properties "Fair wear and tear versus damage in rental properties").

If the issue is not able to be resolved, you or your landlord or agent may need to[take the dispute to the NSW Civil and Administrative Tribunal (NCAT)](https://ncat.nsw.gov.au/case-types/housing-and-property.html "NSW Civil and Administrative Tribunal (https://ncat.nsw.gov.au/case-types/housing-and-property.html)"). This means that the dispute is out of Fair Trading NSW's hands.

To get help, go to the [Tenants’ Union of NSW](https://www.tenants.org.au/ "Tenants' Union of New South Wales (https://www.tenants.org.au/)") for legal advice, assistance, and information to tenants. The Tribunal also provides a useful [list of links to legal help and advice services](https://ncat.nsw.gov.au/help-and-support/get-legal-help-and-advice.html).

If your tenancy is over, you can claim the bond back online

You don’t need to wait for the landlord to release the bond. If you originally submitted your bond online and you have addressed all the things you need to do after ending the tenancy, you can claim the bond on Rental Bonds Online.

[Claim the bond online](https://rbo.fairtrading.nsw.gov.au/tenant/login "Rental Bonds Online registered tenant login (https://rbo.fairtrading.nsw.gov.au/tenant/login)")

Make a complaint to NSW Fair Trading about a bond claim without evidence

If your agent or landlord makes a claim against the bond and does not provide you with evidence of the claim, this is a breach of the Residential Tenancies Act 2010. You should lodge a complaint with NSW Fair Trading to assess their conduct.

[Lodge a complaint with Fair Trading](https://www.nsw.gov.au/housing-and-construction/renting-a-place-to-live/residential-tenancy-complaints "Residential tenancy complaints").

Request advice before a Tribunal hearing

Do you have a date for a hearing in the NSW Civil and Administrative Tribunal (NCAT)? Get advice from your local Tenants Advice and Advocacy Service.

[Use the Tenants' Union request form](https://www.tenants.org.au/ncatadvice)

* * *

retrieved.embedding_text:
Resolving residential tenancy disputes > Repairs, maintenance or damage disputes
If a tenant or landlord is unable to resolve a dispute about repairs, maintenance or damage through [NSW Fair Trading's tenancy and real estate complaint service](https://www.nsw.gov.au/housing-and-construction/renting-a-place-to-live/residential-tenancy-complaints "Residential tenancy complaints"), either party may be able to have the dispute investigated further.

Fair Trading can investigate whether:

*   the landlord has breached their obligation to provide and maintain the property in a reasonable state of repair.
*   the tenant has caused (or permitted) damage to the property and failed to satisfactorily repair the damage without a reasonable excuse.

Fair Trading will then decide whether to issue a [landlord or tenant rectification order](https://www.nsw.gov.au/housing-and-construction/rules/rectification-orders-for-rental-properties "Rectification orders for rental properties") based on these investigations.

The NSW Civil and Administrative Tribunal (the Tribunal) can also make orders relating to repairs, maintenance or damage to the property.

A tenant is not responsible for property damage caused by domestic abuse if they are not the alleged perpetrator of the domestic abuse.

If there is a dispute about whether the damage was caused by domestic abuse, the Tribunal must consider evidence of domestic abuse and make an assessment on the civil standard of proof, known as the balance of probabilities. See [Tenant protections for domestic violence and abuse in a rental property](https://www.nsw.gov.au/housing-and-construction/renting-a-place-to-live/tenant-protections-for-domestic-violence-and-abuse-a-rental-property "Tenant protections for domestic violence and abuse in a rental property") for more information.

What do you need to do?
retrieved.embedding_text:
Getting your bond back at the end of a tenancy > Getting your bond back at the end of a tenancy > What do you need to do?
[](https://www.nsw.gov.au/housing-and-construction/renting-a-place-to-live/getting-your-bond-back)Make sure you have:

*   paid your rent to and including [end of your notice period](https://www.nsw.gov.au/housing-and-construction/rules/minimum-notice-periods-for-ending-a-residential-tenancy "Minimum notice periods for ending a residential tenancy") or your moving date if [breaking lease early](https://www.nsw.gov.au/housing-and-construction/rules/breaking-a-fixed-term-residential-tenancy-early "Breaking a fixed-term residential tenancy early").
*   cleaned your rental property to match its[original condition](https://www.nsw.gov.au/housing-and-construction/rules/rental-property-condition-reports "Property condition at end of tenancy").
*   removed all [your personal things](https://www.nsw.gov.au/housing-and-construction/rules/dealing-goods-left-behind "Dealing with goods left behind").
*   repaired any[damage that was beyond ‘fair wear and tear’](https://www.nsw.gov.au/housing-and-construction/rules/fair-wear-and-tear-versus-damage-rental-properties "Fair wear and tear versus damage in rental properties").
*   signed off on[the condition report](https://www.nsw.gov.au/housing-and-construction/rental-forms-surveys-and-data/resources/residential-tenancy-condition-report "Residential tenancy condition report")with your landlord.
*   returned all [keys and other items](https://www.nsw.gov.au/housing-and-construction/rules/keys-locks-and-security-devices-a-rental-property "Keys, locks and security devices in a rental property")given to you for the property when you moved in.

Now you can claim your refund [using Rental Bonds Online](https://www.nsw.gov.au/housing-and-construction/renting-a-place-to-live/residential-rental-bonds/rental-bonds-online-for-tenants "Rental Bonds Online for tenants"). Your landlord or agent has up to 14 days to accept your claim.

[Log in to Rental Bonds Online](https://rbo.fairtrading.nsw.gov.au/tenant/login "Rental Bonds Online registered tenant login (https://rbo.fairtrading.nsw.gov.au/tenant/login)")

Additional information about getting bond back if:

Expand all Collapse all

You are in a shared tenancy keyboard_arrow_down

The principal tenant who acts on behalf of all co-tenants for the shared rental should

*   submit or respond to a claim for refund of bond money using Rental Bonds Online on behalf of all the tenants at the end of the tenancy.
*   distribute the bond refund to the other tenants.

[Log in to Rental Bonds Online](https://rbo.fairtrading.nsw.gov.au/tenant/login "Rental Bonds Online registered tenant login (https://rbo.fairtrading.nsw.gov.au/tenant/login)") if you are the principal tenant and need to claim the bond.

If a co-tenant moves out of a shared tenancy and requests their bond refund, the remaining tenant/s must pay back their bond – less any rent owed or other reasonable costs – within 14 days of the request.

[Download a change of shared tenancy request form](https://www.nsw.gov.au/housing-and-construction/rental-forms-surveys-and-data/resources/change-of-shared-tenancy-arrangement-form "Change of shared tenancy arrangement form").

This does not apply if:

*   the former co-tenant’s debts exceed the amount of bond money they paid, or
*   the former co-tenant has been excluded from the premises by a final apprehended violence order.

[Learn more about shared tenancies](https://www.nsw.gov.au/housing-and-construction/rules/sharing-a-residential-rental-property "Sharing a residential rental property").

You have a Rentstart bond loan keyboard_arrow_down

If you have repaid your Rentstart bond loan in full before the end of your tenancy, you can claim your bond back at the end of your tenancy.

If your tenancy ends before you have repaid the Rentstart bond loan in full:

*   any funds still owed to the [Department of Communities and Justice (DCJ)](https://dcj.nsw.gov.au/housing.html)will be returned to them from the bond, and
*   any amounts you have repaid will be returned directly to you, less any amount still owed to the agent or landlord.

If a claim is made against the bond that you do not agree with, you can still challenge this claim regardless of whether the loan has been repaid in full.

[Get more information about Rentstart](https://www.nsw.gov.au/housing-and-construction/renting-a-place-to-live/financial-support#toc-rentstart).

You need to get the bond back before the end of your tenancy keyboard_arrow_down

You can only claim a bond refund before the end of a tenancy if:

*   you have a written agreement from your landlord or agent to submit an earlier claim, or

*   you are directing the full bond to go to your landlord or property agent.

There are very specific legal reasons to end a tenancy early. Otherwise, you could breach the terms of your tenancy agreement.

Get more information about [ending a tenancy](https://www.nsw.gov.au/housing-and-construction/renting-a-place-to-live/ending-a-residential-tenancy "Ending a residential tenancy")and [minimum notice periods](https://www.nsw.gov.au/housing-and-construction/rules/minimum-notice-periods-for-ending-a-residential-tenancy "Minimum notice periods for ending a residential tenancy") that apply.

You need to claim your bond refund on paper keyboard_arrow_down

If you don't have a Rental Bonds Online account, you can fill in a ‘Claim for Bond Refund’ paper form from NSW Fair Trading.

1.   [Download the Claim for Bond Refund form](https://www.nsw.gov.au/housing-and-construction/rental-forms-surveys-and-data/resources/claim-for-refund-of-bond-money-form "NSW Fair Trading claim for refund of bond money form (https://www.fairtrading.nsw.gov.au/__data/assets/pdf_file/0009/367749/Claim-for-Bond-Refund-form.pdf)").
2.   Sign the completed form with the landlord or agent.
3.   Return the form to NSW Fair Trading by 
    *   post (address on form)
    *   email[bondclaims@customerservice.nsw.gov.au](mailto:bondclaims@customerservice.nsw.gov.au)
    *   or in person (details of where to lodge are on the form).

Fair Trading will give the landlord or agent written notice that you have made a claim.

If your landlord or agent fails to sign the form, you can still submit it. They are given 14 days to dispute your claim.

If the landlord or agent doesn't dispute your claim, Fair Trading will pay your claim after 14 days.

Your money will be deposited into your bank account.

* * *

retrieved.embedding_text:
Resolving residential tenancy disputes > Rental bond disputes
A claim for a rental bond can be submitted by either the tenant or the landlord or agent once the tenancy has ended, [but only if the status of the bond is "HELD"](https://www.nsw.gov.au/housing-and-construction/renting-a-place-to-live/residential-rental-bonds/rental-bonds-online-for-tenants "Rental Bonds Online for tenants") in Rental Bonds Online.

If a tenant doesn't agree with a [landlord's or agent's claim on their bond](https://www.nsw.gov.au/housing-and-construction/landlords/rental-bonds-online-for-landlords "Rental Bonds Online for self-managing landlords"), the tenant should try to talk to their landlord or agent about what could be done to deal with the dispute and try to come to an agreement.

If they cannot come to an agreement, they need to apply to the Tribunal and [notify NSW Rental Bonds](https://www.nsw.gov.au/housing-and-construction/renting-a-place-to-live/residential-rental-bonds/rental-bonds-online-for-tenants "Rental Bonds Online for tenants"), before the 'due for payment' date.

When a co-tenant moves out, they can ask the remaining co-tenants to repay their share of the rental bond. If the bond share is not repaid within 14 days, the former co-tenant may [apply to the Tribunal for an order about how the bond should be paid between the co-tenants](https://www.nsw.gov.au/housing-and-construction/rules/sharing-a-residential-rental-property#toc-claiming-the-rental-bond-at-the-end-of-a-shared-tenancy "Tribunal for an order about how the bond should be paid between the co-tenants").

If you have left your tenancy because of domestic abuse, see [Tenant protections for domestic violence and abuse in a rental property](https://www.nsw.gov.au/housing-and-construction/renting-a-place-to-live/tenant-protections-for-domestic-violence-and-abuse-a-rental-property "Tenant protections for domestic violence and abuse in a rental property") for information about getting your rental bond back.

Getting your bond back at the end of a tenancy > Getting your bond back at the end of a tenancy > When and where you will get your refund
If you are using Rental Bonds Online and all your details are correct, you should get your bond back in two business days after your claim is accepted by your landlord or agent.

Refunds from Rental Bonds Online are paid by direct deposit into your nominated bank account.

[Make sure your bank account details are up to date](https://www.nsw.gov.au/housing-and-construction/renting-a-place-to-live/residential-rental-bonds/rental-bonds-online-for-tenants#toc-what-you-need-to-access-rbo "Rental Bonds Online for tenants")

retrieved.embedding_text:
Getting your bond back at the end of a tenancy > Getting your bond back at the end of a tenancy > What if things go wrong?
Things may go wrong if

*   you have not addressed all the things you need to do when ending a tenancy
*   you have a disagreement with your landlord or agent and need to negotiate
*   your [landlord or agent disputes your claim](https://www.nsw.gov.au/housing-and-construction/renting-a-place-to-live/residential-rental-bonds/dealing-bond-disputes-for-tenants "Dealing with bond disputes for tenants")
*   you cannot afford to pay for [damages beyond fair wear and tear](https://www.nsw.gov.au/housing-and-construction/rules/fair-wear-and-tear-versus-damage-rental-properties "Fair wear and tear versus damage in rental properties").

If the issue is not able to be resolved, you or your landlord or agent may need to[take the dispute to the NSW Civil and Administrative Tribunal (NCAT)](https://ncat.nsw.gov.au/case-types/housing-and-property.html "NSW Civil and Administrative Tribunal (https://ncat.nsw.gov.au/case-types/housing-and-property.html)"). This means that the dispute is out of Fair Trading NSW's hands.

To get help, go to the [Tenants’ Union of NSW](https://www.tenants.org.au/ "Tenants' Union of New South Wales (https://www.tenants.org.au/)") for legal advice, assistance, and information to tenants. The Tribunal also provides a useful [list of links to legal help and advice services](https://ncat.nsw.gov.au/help-and-support/get-legal-help-and-advice.html).

If your tenancy is over, you can claim the bond back online

You don’t need to wait for the landlord to release the bond. If you originally submitted your bond online and you have addressed all the things you need to do after ending the tenancy, you can claim the bond on Rental Bonds Online.

[Claim the bond online](https://rbo.fairtrading.nsw.gov.au/tenant/login "Rental Bonds Online registered tenant login (https://rbo.fairtrading.nsw.gov.au/tenant/login)")

Make a complaint to NSW Fair Trading about a bond claim without evidence

If your agent or landlord makes a claim against the bond and does not provide you with evidence of the claim, this is a breach of the Residential Tenancies Act 2010. You should lodge a complaint with NSW Fair Trading to assess their conduct.

[Lodge a complaint with Fair Trading](https://www.nsw.gov.au/housing-and-construction/renting-a-place-to-live/residential-tenancy-complaints "Residential tenancy complaints").

Request advice before a Tribunal hearing

Do you have a date for a hearing in the NSW Civil and Administrative Tribunal (NCAT)? Get advice from your local Tenants Advice and Advocacy Service.

[Use the Tenants' Union request form](https://www.tenants.org.au/ncatadvice)

* * *

*   you have not addressed all the things you need to do when ending a tenancy
*   you have a disagreement with your landlord or agent and need to negotiate
*   your [landlord or agent disputes your claim](https://www.nsw.gov.au/housing-and-construction/renting-a-place-to-live/residential-rental-bonds/dealing-bond-disputes-for-tenants "Dealing with bond disputes for tenants")
*   you cannot afford to pay for [damages beyond fair wear and tear](https://www.nsw.gov.au/housing-and-construction/rules/fair-wear-and-tear-versus-damage-rental-properties "Fair wear and tear versus damage in rental properties").

If the issue is not able to be resolved, you or your landlord or agent may need to[take the dispute to the NSW Civil and Administrative Tribunal (NCAT)](https://ncat.nsw.gov.au/case-types/housing-and-property.html "NSW Civil and Administrative Tribunal (https://ncat.nsw.gov.au/case-types/housing-and-property.html)"). This means that the dispute is out of Fair Trading NSW's hands.

To get help, go to the [Tenants’ Union of NSW](https://www.tenants.org.au/ "Tenants' Union of New South Wales (https://www.tenants.org.au/)") for legal advice, assistance, and information to tenants. The Tribunal also provides a useful [list of links to legal help and advice services](https://ncat.nsw.gov.au/help-and-support/get-legal-help-and-advice.html).

If your tenancy is over, you can claim the bond back online

You don’t need to wait for the landlord to release the bond. If you originally submitted your bond online and you have addressed all the things you need to do after ending the tenancy, you can claim the bond on Rental Bonds Online.

[Claim the bond online](https://rbo.fairtrading.nsw.gov.au/tenant/login "Rental Bonds Online registered tenant login (https://rbo.fairtrading.nsw.gov.au/tenant/login)")

Make a complaint to NSW Fair Trading about a bond claim without evidence

If your agent or landlord makes a claim against the bond and does not provide you with evidence of the claim, this is a breach of the Residential Tenancies Act 2010. You should lodge a complaint with NSW Fair Trading to assess their conduct.

[Lodge a complaint with Fair Trading](https://www.nsw.gov.au/housing-and-construction/renting-a-place-to-live/residential-tenancy-complaints "Residential tenancy complaints").

Request advice before a Tribunal hearing

Do you have a date for a hearing in the NSW Civil and Administrative Tribunal (NCAT)? Get advice from your local Tenants Advice and Advocacy Service.

[Use the Tenants' Union request form](https://www.tenants.org.au/ncatadvice)

* * *

Resolving residential tenancy disputes > Resolving disputes through the Tribunal
The Tribunal is an independent body that hears and decides on applications for orders from tenants and landlords.

A landlord or tenant can apply directly to the Tribunal for orders relating to a residential tenancy instead of first [making a complaint to Fair Trading](https://www.nsw.gov.au/housing-and-construction/renting-a-place-to-live/residential-tenancy-complaints "Tenancy complaints"), if they wish.

A landlord or tenant can decide to lodge an application with the Tribunal if:

*   Fair Trading cannot find a solution mutually agreed to by both parties.
*   A termination order is being sought.
*   The complaint relates to a matter for which Fair Trading is not able to offer dispute resolution, such as a dispute relating to claiming a bond.

The optional break fee clause will not apply if the break fee clause has been deleted from the tenancy agreement.

A landlord may still seek compensation by applying to the Tribunal.

These costs may include:

*   loss of rent
*   advertising
*   a letting fee if the landlord uses an agent.

The landlord or agent may negotiate an agreed amount of compensation with the tenant.

If the tenant and landlord are unable to agree on the amount of compensation, the landlord may claim from the bond or apply to the Tribunal for an order that the tenant pays the landlord a certain amount of compensation.

The landlord will need to show the Tribunal what (reasonable) steps they took to minimise their losses (e.g. advertising for a new tenant without delay).

retrieved.embedding_text:
Resolving residential tenancy disputes > Rental bond disputes
A claim for a rental bond can be submitted by either the tenant or the landlord or agent once the tenancy has ended, [but only if the status of the bond is "HELD"](https://www.nsw.gov.au/housing-and-construction/renting-a-place-to-live/residential-rental-bonds/rental-bonds-online-for-tenants "Rental Bonds Online for tenants") in Rental Bonds Online.

If a tenant doesn't agree with a [landlord's or agent's claim on their bond](https://www.nsw.gov.au/housing-and-construction/landlords/rental-bonds-online-for-landlords "Rental Bonds Online for self-managing landlords"), the tenant should try to talk to their landlord or agent about what could be done to deal with the dispute and try to come to an agreement.

If they cannot come to an agreement, they need to apply to the Tribunal and [notify NSW Rental Bonds](https://www.nsw.gov.au/housing-and-construction/renting-a-place-to-live/residential-rental-bonds/rental-bonds-online-for-tenants "Rental Bonds Online for tenants"), before the 'due for payment' date.

When a co-tenant moves out, they can ask the remaining co-tenants to repay their share of the rental bond. If the bond share is not repaid within 14 days, the former co-tenant may [apply to the Tribunal for an order about how the bond should be paid between the co-tenants](https://www.nsw.gov.au/housing-and-construction/rules/sharing-a-residential-rental-property#toc-claiming-the-rental-bond-at-the-end-of-a-shared-tenancy "Tribunal for an order about how the bond should be paid between the co-tenants").

If you have left your tenancy because of domestic abuse, see [Tenant protections for domestic violence and abuse in a rental property](https://www.nsw.gov.au/housing-and-construction/renting-a-place-to-live/tenant-protections-for-domestic-violence-and-abuse-a-rental-property "Tenant protections for domestic violence and abuse in a rental property") for information about getting your rental bond back.

What do you need to do?
retrieved.embedding_text:
Getting your bond back at the end of a tenancy > Getting your bond back at the end of a tenancy > What do you need to do?
[](https://www.nsw.gov.au/housing-and-construction/renting-a-place-to-live/getting-your-bond-back)Make sure you have:

*   paid your rent to and including [end of your notice period](https://www.nsw.gov.au/housing-and-construction/rules/minimum-notice-periods-for-ending-a-residential-tenancy "Minimum notice periods for ending a residential tenancy") or your moving date if [breaking lease early](https://www.nsw.gov.au/housing-and-construction/rules/breaking-a-fixed-term-residential-tenancy-early "Breaking a fixed-term residential tenancy early").
*   cleaned your rental property to match its[original condition](https://www.nsw.gov.au/housing-and-construction/rules/rental-property-condition-reports "Property condition at end of tenancy").
*   removed all [your personal things](https://www.nsw.gov.au/housing-and-construction/rules/dealing-goods-left-behind "Dealing with goods left behind").
*   repaired any[damage that was beyond ‘fair wear and tear’](https://www.nsw.gov.au/housing-and-construction/rules/fair-wear-and-tear-versus-damage-rental-properties "Fair wear and tear versus damage in rental properties").
*   signed off on[the condition report](https://www.nsw.gov.au/housing-and-construction/rental-forms-surveys-and-data/resources/residential-tenancy-condition-report "Residential tenancy condition report")with your landlord.
*   returned all [keys and other items](https://www.nsw.gov.au/housing-and-construction/rules/keys-locks-and-security-devices-a-rental-property "Keys, locks and security devices in a rental property")given to you for the property when you moved in.

Now you can claim your refund [using Rental Bonds Online](https://www.nsw.gov.au/housing-and-construction/renting-a-place-to-live/residential-rental-bonds/rental-bonds-online-for-tenants "Rental Bonds Online for tenants"). Your landlord or agent has up to 14 days to accept your claim.

[Log in to Rental Bonds Online](https://rbo.fairtrading.nsw.gov.au/tenant/login "Rental Bonds Online registered tenant login (https://rbo.fairtrading.nsw.gov.au/tenant/login)")

Additional information about getting bond back if:

Expand all Collapse all

You are in a shared tenancy keyboard_arrow_down

The principal tenant who acts on behalf of all co-tenants for the shared rental should

*   submit or respond to a claim for refund of bond money using Rental Bonds Online on behalf of all the tenants at the end of the tenancy.
*   distribute the bond refund to the other tenants.

[Log in to Rental Bonds Online](https://rbo.fairtrading.nsw.gov.au/tenant/login "Rental Bonds Online registered tenant login (https://rbo.fairtrading.nsw.gov.au/tenant/login)") if you are the principal tenant and need to claim the bond.

If a co-tenant moves out of a shared tenancy and requests their bond refund, the remaining tenant/s must pay back their bond – less any rent owed or other reasonable costs – within 14 days of the request.

[Download a change of shared tenancy request form](https://www.nsw.gov.au/housing-and-construction/rental-forms-surveys-and-data/resources/change-of-shared-tenancy-arrangement-form "Change of shared tenancy arrangement form").

This does not apply if:

*   the former co-tenant’s debts exceed the amount of bond money they paid, or
*   the former co-tenant has been excluded from the premises by a final apprehended violence order.

[Learn more about shared tenancies](https://www.nsw.gov.au/housing-and-construction/rules/sharing-a-residential-rental-property "Sharing a residential rental property").

You have a Rentstart bond loan keyboard_arrow_down

If you have repaid your Rentstart bond loan in full before the end of your tenancy, you can claim your bond back at the end of your tenancy.

If your tenancy ends before you have repaid the Rentstart bond loan in full:

*   any funds still owed to the [Department of Communities and Justice (DCJ)](https://dcj.nsw.gov.au/housing.html)will be returned to them from the bond, and
*   any amounts you have repaid will be returned directly to you, less any amount still owed to the agent or landlord.

If a claim is made against the bond that you do not agree with, you can still challenge this claim regardless of whether the loan has been repaid in full.

[Get more information about Rentstart](https://www.nsw.gov.au/housing-and-construction/renting-a-place-to-live/financial-support#toc-rentstart).

You need to get the bond back before the end of your tenancy keyboard_arrow_down

You can only claim a bond refund before the end of a tenancy if:

*   you have a written agreement from your landlord or agent to submit an earlier claim, or

*   you are directing the full bond to go to your landlord or property agent.

There are very specific legal reasons to end a tenancy early. Otherwise, you could breach the terms of your tenancy agreement.

Get more information about [ending a tenancy](https://www.nsw.gov.au/housing-and-construction/renting-a-place-to-live/ending-a-residential-tenancy "Ending a residential tenancy")and [minimum notice periods](https://www.nsw.gov.au/housing-and-construction/rules/minimum-notice-periods-for-ending-a-residential-tenancy "Minimum notice periods for ending a residential tenancy") that apply.

You need to claim your bond refund on paper keyboard_arrow_down

If you don't have a Rental Bonds Online account, you can fill in a ‘Claim for Bond Refund’ paper form from NSW Fair Trading.

1.   [Download the Claim for Bond Refund form](https://www.nsw.gov.au/housing-and-construction/rental-forms-surveys-and-data/resources/claim-for-refund-of-bond-money-form "NSW Fair Trading claim for refund of bond money form (https://www.fairtrading.nsw.gov.au/__data/assets/pdf_file/0009/367749/Claim-for-Bond-Refund-form.pdf)").
2.   Sign the completed form with the landlord or agent.
3.   Return the form to NSW Fair Trading by 
    *   post (address on form)
    *   email[bondclaims@customerservice.nsw.gov.au](mailto:bondclaims@customerservice.nsw.gov.au)
    *   or in person (details of where to lodge are on the form).

Fair Trading will give the landlord or agent written notice that you have made a claim.

If your landlord or agent fails to sign the form, you can still submit it. They are given 14 days to dispute your claim.

If the landlord or agent doesn't dispute your claim, Fair Trading will pay your claim after 14 days.

Your money will be deposited into your bank account.

* * *

Getting your bond back at the end of a tenancy > Getting your bond back at the end of a tenancy > What if things go wrong?
Things may go wrong if

*   you have not addressed all the things you need to do when ending a tenancy
*   you have a disagreement with your landlord or agent and need to negotiate
*   your [landlord or agent disputes your claim](https://www.nsw.gov.au/housing-and-construction/renting-a-place-to-live/residential-rental-bonds/dealing-bond-disputes-for-tenants "Dealing with bond disputes for tenants")
*   you cannot afford to pay for [damages beyond fair wear and tear](https://www.nsw.gov.au/housing-and-construction/rules/fair-wear-and-tear-versus-damage-rental-properties "Fair wear and tear versus damage in rental properties").

If the issue is not able to be resolved, you or your landlord or agent may need to[take the dispute to the NSW Civil and Administrative Tribunal (NCAT)](https://ncat.nsw.gov.au/case-types/housing-and-property.html "NSW Civil and Administrative Tribunal (https://ncat.nsw.gov.au/case-types/housing-and-property.html)"). This means that the dispute is out of Fair Trading NSW's hands.

To get help, go to the [Tenants’ Union of NSW](https://www.tenants.org.au/ "Tenants' Union of New South Wales (https://www.tenants.org.au/)") for legal advice, assistance, and information to tenants. The Tribunal also provides a useful [list of links to legal help and advice services](https://ncat.nsw.gov.au/help-and-support/get-legal-help-and-advice.html).

If your tenancy is over, you can claim the bond back online

You don’t need to wait for the landlord to release the bond. If you originally submitted your bond online and you have addressed all the things you need to do after ending the tenancy, you can claim the bond on Rental Bonds Online.

[Claim the bond online](https://rbo.fairtrading.nsw.gov.au/tenant/login "Rental Bonds Online registered tenant login (https://rbo.fairtrading.nsw.gov.au/tenant/login)")

Make a complaint to NSW Fair Trading about a bond claim without evidence

If your agent or landlord makes a claim against the bond and does not provide you with evidence of the claim, this is a breach of the Residential Tenancies Act 2010. You should lodge a complaint with NSW Fair Trading to assess their conduct.

[Lodge a complaint with Fair Trading](https://www.nsw.gov.au/housing-and-construction/renting-a-place-to-live/residential-tenancy-complaints "Residential tenancy complaints").

Request advice before a Tribunal hearing

Do you have a date for a hearing in the NSW Civil and Administrative Tribunal (NCAT)? Get advice from your local Tenants Advice and Advocacy Service.

[Use the Tenants' Union request form](https://www.tenants.org.au/ncatadvice)

What do you need to do?
retrieved.embedding_text:
Getting your bond back at the end of a tenancy > Getting your bond back at the end of a tenancy > What do you need to do?
[](https://www.nsw.gov.au/housing-and-construction/renting-a-place-to-live/getting-your-bond-back)Make sure you have:

*   paid your rent to and including [end of your notice period](https://www.nsw.gov.au/housing-and-construction/rules/minimum-notice-periods-for-ending-a-residential-tenancy "Minimum notice periods for ending a residential tenancy") or your moving date if [breaking lease early](https://www.nsw.gov.au/housing-and-construction/rules/breaking-a-fixed-term-residential-tenancy-early "Breaking a fixed-term residential tenancy early").
*   cleaned your rental property to match its[original condition](https://www.nsw.gov.au/housing-and-construction/rules/rental-property-condition-reports "Property condition at end of tenancy").
*   removed all [your personal things](https://www.nsw.gov.au/housing-and-construction/rules/dealing-goods-left-behind "Dealing with goods left behind").
*   repaired any[damage that was beyond ‘fair wear and tear’](https://www.nsw.gov.au/housing-and-construction/rules/fair-wear-and-tear-versus-damage-rental-properties "Fair wear and tear versus damage in rental properties").
*   signed off on[the condition report](https://www.nsw.gov.au/housing-and-construction/rental-forms-surveys-and-data/resources/residential-tenancy-condition-report "Residential tenancy condition report")with your landlord.
*   returned all [keys and other items](https://www.nsw.gov.au/housing-and-construction/rules/keys-locks-and-security-devices-a-rental-property "Keys, locks and security devices in a rental property")given to you for the property when you moved in.

Now you can claim your refund [using Rental Bonds Online](https://www.nsw.gov.au/housing-and-construction/renting-a-place-to-live/residential-rental-bonds/rental-bonds-online-for-tenants "Rental Bonds Online for tenants"). Your landlord or agent has up to 14 days to accept your claim.

[Log in to Rental Bonds Online](https://rbo.fairtrading.nsw.gov.au/tenant/login "Rental Bonds Online registered tenant login (https://rbo.fairtrading.nsw.gov.au/tenant/login)")

Additional information about getting bond back if:

Expand all Collapse all

You are in a shared tenancy keyboard_arrow_down

The principal tenant who acts on behalf of all co-tenants for the shared rental should

*   submit or respond to a claim for refund of bond money using Rental Bonds Online on behalf of all the tenants at the end of the tenancy.
*   distribute the bond refund to the other tenants.

[Log in to Rental Bonds Online](https://rbo.fairtrading.nsw.gov.au/tenant/login "Rental Bonds Online registered tenant login (https://rbo.fairtrading.nsw.gov.au/tenant/login)") if you are the principal tenant and need to claim the bond.

If a co-tenant moves out of a shared tenancy and requests their bond refund, the remaining tenant/s must pay back their bond – less any rent owed or other reasonable costs – within 14 days of the request.

[Download a change of shared tenancy request form](https://www.nsw.gov.au/housing-and-construction/rental-forms-surveys-and-data/resources/change-of-shared-tenancy-arrangement-form "Change of shared tenancy arrangement form").

This does not apply if:

*   the former co-tenant’s debts exceed the amount of bond money they paid, or
*   the former co-tenant has been excluded from the premises by a final apprehended violence order.

[Learn more about shared tenancies](https://www.nsw.gov.au/housing-and-construction/rules/sharing-a-residential-rental-property "Sharing a residential rental property").

You have a Rentstart bond loan keyboard_arrow_down

If you have repaid your Rentstart bond loan in full before the end of your tenancy, you can claim your bond back at the end of your tenancy.

If your tenancy ends before you have repaid the Rentstart bond loan in full:

*   any funds still owed to the [Department of Communities and Justice (DCJ)](https://dcj.nsw.gov.au/housing.html)will be returned to them from the bond, and
*   any amounts you have repaid will be returned directly to you, less any amount still owed to the agent or landlord.

If a claim is made against the bond that you do not agree with, you can still challenge this claim regardless of whether the loan has been repaid in full.

[Get more information about Rentstart](https://www.nsw.gov.au/housing-and-construction/renting-a-place-to-live/financial-support#toc-rentstart).

You need to get the bond back before the end of your tenancy keyboard_arrow_down

You can only claim a bond refund before the end of a tenancy if:

*   you have a written agreement from your landlord or agent to submit an earlier claim, or

*   you are directing the full bond to go to your landlord or property agent.

There are very specific legal reasons to end a tenancy early. Otherwise, you could breach the terms of your tenancy agreement.

Get more information about [ending a tenancy](https://www.nsw.gov.au/housing-and-construction/renting-a-place-to-live/ending-a-residential-tenancy "Ending a residential tenancy")and [minimum notice periods](https://www.nsw.gov.au/housing-and-construction/rules/minimum-notice-periods-for-ending-a-residential-tenancy "Minimum notice periods for ending a residential tenancy") that apply.

You need to claim your bond refund on paper keyboard_arrow_down

If you don't have a Rental Bonds Online account, you can fill in a ‘Claim for Bond Refund’ paper form from NSW Fair Trading.

1.   [Download the Claim for Bond Refund form](https://www.nsw.gov.au/housing-and-construction/rental-forms-surveys-and-data/resources/claim-for-refund-of-bond-money-form "NSW Fair Trading claim for refund of bond money form (https://www.fairtrading.nsw.gov.au/__data/assets/pdf_file/0009/367749/Claim-for-Bond-Refund-form.pdf)").
2.   Sign the completed form with the landlord or agent.
3.   Return the form to NSW Fair Trading by 
    *   post (address on form)
    *   email[bondclaims@customerservice.nsw.gov.au](mailto:bondclaims@customerservice.nsw.gov.au)
    *   or in person (details of where to lodge are on the form).

Fair Trading will give the landlord or agent written notice that you have made a claim.

If your landlord or agent fails to sign the form, you can still submit it. They are given 14 days to dispute your claim.

If the landlord or agent doesn't dispute your claim, Fair Trading will pay your claim after 14 days.

Your money will be deposited into your bank account.

* * *

retrieved.embedding_text:
Resolving residential tenancy disputes > Rental bond disputes
A claim for a rental bond can be submitted by either the tenant or the landlord or agent once the tenancy has ended, [but only if the status of the bond is "HELD"](https://www.nsw.gov.au/housing-and-construction/renting-a-place-to-live/residential-rental-bonds/rental-bonds-online-for-tenants "Rental Bonds Online for tenants") in Rental Bonds Online.

If a tenant doesn't agree with a [landlord's or agent's claim on their bond](https://www.nsw.gov.au/housing-and-construction/landlords/rental-bonds-online-for-landlords "Rental Bonds Online for self-managing landlords"), the tenant should try to talk to their landlord or agent about what could be done to deal with the dispute and try to come to an agreement.

If they cannot come to an agreement, they need to apply to the Tribunal and [notify NSW Rental Bonds](https://www.nsw.gov.au/housing-and-construction/renting-a-place-to-live/residential-rental-bonds/rental-bonds-online-for-tenants "Rental Bonds Online for tenants"), before the 'due for payment' date.

When a co-tenant moves out, they can ask the remaining co-tenants to repay their share of the rental bond. If the bond share is not repaid within 14 days, the former co-tenant may [apply to the Tribunal for an order about how the bond should be paid between the co-tenants](https://www.nsw.gov.au/housing-and-construction/rules/sharing-a-residential-rental-property#toc-claiming-the-rental-bond-at-the-end-of-a-shared-tenancy "Tribunal for an order about how the bond should be paid between the co-tenants").

If you have left your tenancy because of domestic abuse, see [Tenant protections for domestic violence and abuse in a rental property](https://www.nsw.gov.au/housing-and-construction/renting-a-place-to-live/tenant-protections-for-domestic-violence-and-abuse-a-rental-property "Tenant protections for domestic violence and abuse in a rental property") for information about getting your rental bond back.

[Use the Tenants' Union request form](https://www.tenants.org.au/ncatadvice)

The optional break fee clause will not apply if the break fee clause has been deleted from the tenancy agreement.

A landlord may still seek compensation by applying to the Tribunal.

These costs may include:

*   loss of rent
*   advertising
*   a letting fee if the landlord uses an agent.

The landlord or agent may negotiate an agreed amount of compensation with the tenant.

If the tenant and landlord are unable to agree on the amount of compensation, the landlord may claim from the bond or apply to the Tribunal for an order that the tenant pays the landlord a certain amount of compensation.

retrieved.embedding_text:
Resolving residential tenancy disputes > Resolving disputes through the Tribunal
The Tribunal is an independent body that hears and decides on applications for orders from tenants and landlords.

A landlord or tenant can apply directly to the Tribunal for orders relating to a residential tenancy instead of first [making a complaint to Fair Trading](https://www.nsw.gov.au/housing-and-construction/renting-a-place-to-live/residential-tenancy-complaints "Tenancy complaints"), if they wish.

A landlord or tenant can decide to lodge an application with the Tribunal if:

*   Fair Trading cannot find a solution mutually agreed to by both parties.
*   A termination order is being sought.
*   The complaint relates to a matter for which Fair Trading is not able to offer dispute resolution, such as a dispute relating to claiming a bond.

What do you need to do?
retrieved.embedding_text:
Getting your bond back at the end of a tenancy > Getting your bond back at the end of a tenancy > What do you need to do?
[](https://www.nsw.gov.au/housing-and-construction/renting-a-place-to-live/getting-your-bond-back)Make sure you have:

*   paid your rent to and including [end of your notice period](https://www.nsw.gov.au/housing-and-construction/rules/minimum-notice-periods-for-ending-a-residential-tenancy "Minimum notice periods for ending a residential tenancy") or your moving date if [breaking lease early](https://www.nsw.gov.au/housing-and-construction/rules/breaking-a-fixed-term-residential-tenancy-early "Breaking a fixed-term residential tenancy early").
*   cleaned your rental property to match its[original condition](https://www.nsw.gov.au/housing-and-construction/rules/rental-property-condition-reports "Property condition at end of tenancy").
*   removed all [your personal things](https://www.nsw.gov.au/housing-and-construction/rules/dealing-goods-left-behind "Dealing with goods left behind").
*   repaired any[damage that was beyond ‘fair wear and tear’](https://www.nsw.gov.au/housing-and-construction/rules/fair-wear-and-tear-versus-damage-rental-properties "Fair wear and tear versus damage in rental properties").
*   signed off on[the condition report](https://www.nsw.gov.au/housing-and-construction/rental-forms-surveys-and-data/resources/residential-tenancy-condition-report "Residential tenancy condition report")with your landlord.
*   returned all [keys and other items](https://www.nsw.gov.au/housing-and-construction/rules/keys-locks-and-security-devices-a-rental-property "Keys, locks and security devices in a rental property")given to you for the property when you moved in.

Now you can claim your refund [using Rental Bonds Online](https://www.nsw.gov.au/housing-and-construction/renting-a-place-to-live/residential-rental-bonds/rental-bonds-online-for-tenants "Rental Bonds Online for tenants"). Your landlord or agent has up to 14 days to accept your claim.

[Log in to Rental Bonds Online](https://rbo.fairtrading.nsw.gov.au/tenant/login "Rental Bonds Online registered tenant login (https://rbo.fairtrading.nsw.gov.au/tenant/login)")

Additional information about getting bond back if:

Expand all Collapse all

You are in a shared tenancy keyboard_arrow_down

The principal tenant who acts on behalf of all co-tenants for the shared rental should

*   submit or respond to a claim for refund of bond money using Rental Bonds Online on behalf of all the tenants at the end of the tenancy.
*   distribute the bond refund to the other tenants.

[Log in to Rental Bonds Online](https://rbo.fairtrading.nsw.gov.au/tenant/login "Rental Bonds Online registered tenant login (https://rbo.fairtrading.nsw.gov.au/tenant/login)") if you are the principal tenant and need to claim the bond.

If a co-tenant moves out of a shared tenancy and requests their bond refund, the remaining tenant/s must pay back their bond – less any rent owed or other reasonable costs – within 14 days of the request.

[Download a change of shared tenancy request form](https://www.nsw.gov.au/housing-and-construction/rental-forms-surveys-and-data/resources/change-of-shared-tenancy-arrangement-form "Change of shared tenancy arrangement form").

This does not apply if:

*   the former co-tenant’s debts exceed the amount of bond money they paid, or
*   the former co-tenant has been excluded from the premises by a final apprehended violence order.

[Learn more about shared tenancies](https://www.nsw.gov.au/housing-and-construction/rules/sharing-a-residential-rental-property "Sharing a residential rental property").

You have a Rentstart bond loan keyboard_arrow_down

If you have repaid your Rentstart bond loan in full before the end of your tenancy, you can claim your bond back at the end of your tenancy.

If your tenancy ends before you have repaid the Rentstart bond loan in full:

*   any funds still owed to the [Department of Communities and Justice (DCJ)](https://dcj.nsw.gov.au/housing.html)will be returned to them from the bond, and
*   any amounts you have repaid will be returned directly to you, less any amount still owed to the agent or landlord.

If a claim is made against the bond that you do not agree with, you can still challenge this claim regardless of whether the loan has been repaid in full.

[Get more information about Rentstart](https://www.nsw.gov.au/housing-and-construction/renting-a-place-to-live/financial-support#toc-rentstart).

You need to get the bond back before the end of your tenancy keyboard_arrow_down

You can only claim a bond refund before the end of a tenancy if:

*   you have a written agreement from your landlord or agent to submit an earlier claim, or

*   you are directing the full bond to go to your landlord or property agent.

There are very specific legal reasons to end a tenancy early. Otherwise, you could breach the terms of your tenancy agreement.

Get more information about [ending a tenancy](https://www.nsw.gov.au/housing-and-construction/renting-a-place-to-live/ending-a-residential-tenancy "Ending a residential tenancy")and [minimum notice periods](https://www.nsw.gov.au/housing-and-construction/rules/minimum-notice-periods-for-ending-a-residential-tenancy "Minimum notice periods for ending a residential tenancy") that apply.

You need to claim your bond refund on paper keyboard_arrow_down

If you don't have a Rental Bonds Online account, you can fill in a ‘Claim for Bond Refund’ paper form from NSW Fair Trading.

1.   [Download the Claim for Bond Refund form](https://www.nsw.gov.au/housing-and-construction/rental-forms-surveys-and-data/resources/claim-for-refund-of-bond-money-form "NSW Fair Trading claim for refund of bond money form (https://www.fairtrading.nsw.gov.au/__data/assets/pdf_file/0009/367749/Claim-for-Bond-Refund-form.pdf)").
2.   Sign the completed form with the landlord or agent.
3.   Return the form to NSW Fair Trading by 
    *   post (address on form)
    *   email[bondclaims@customerservice.nsw.gov.au](mailto:bondclaims@customerservice.nsw.gov.au)
    *   or in person (details of where to lodge are on the form).

Fair Trading will give the landlord or agent written notice that you have made a claim.

If your landlord or agent fails to sign the form, you can still submit it. They are given 14 days to dispute your claim.

If the landlord or agent doesn't dispute your claim, Fair Trading will pay your claim after 14 days.

Your money will be deposited into your bank account.

* * *

*   you cannot afford to pay for [damages beyond fair wear and tear](https://www.nsw.gov.au/housing-and-construction/rules/fair-wear-and-tear-versus-damage-rental-properties "Fair wear and tear versus damage in rental properties").

If the issue is not able to be resolved, you or your landlord or agent may need to[take the dispute to the NSW Civil and Administrative Tribunal (NCAT)](https://ncat.nsw.gov.au/case-types/housing-and-property.html "NSW Civil and Administrative Tribunal (https://ncat.nsw.gov.au/case-types/housing-and-property.html)"). This means that the dispute is out of Fair Trading NSW's hands.

To get help, go to the [Tenants’ Union of NSW](https://www.tenants.org.au/ "Tenants' Union of New South Wales (https://www.tenants.org.au/)") for legal advice, assistance, and information to tenants. The Tribunal also provides a useful [list of links to legal help and advice services](https://ncat.nsw.gov.au/help-and-support/get-legal-help-and-advice.html).

If your tenancy is over, you can claim the bond back online

You don’t need to wait for the landlord to release the bond. If you originally submitted your bond online and you have addressed all the things you need to do after ending the tenancy, you can claim the bond on Rental Bonds Online.

[Claim the bond online](https://rbo.fairtrading.nsw.gov.au/tenant/login "Rental Bonds Online registered tenant login (https://rbo.fairtrading.nsw.gov.au/tenant/login)")

Make a complaint to NSW Fair Trading about a bond claim without evidence

If your agent or landlord makes a claim against the bond and does not provide you with evidence of the claim, this is a breach of the Residential Tenancies Act 2010. You should lodge a complaint with NSW Fair Trading to assess their conduct.

[Lodge a complaint with Fair Trading](https://www.nsw.gov.au/housing-and-construction/renting-a-place-to-live/residential-tenancy-complaints "Residential tenancy complaints").

Request advice before a Tribunal hearing

Do you have a date for a hearing in the NSW Civil and Administrative Tribunal (NCAT)? Get advice from your local Tenants Advice and Advocacy Service.

[Use the Tenants' Union request form](https://www.tenants.org.au/ncatadvice)

* * *

retrieved.embedding_text:
Resolving residential tenancy disputes > Rental bond disputes
A claim for a rental bond can be submitted by either the tenant or the landlord or agent once the tenancy has ended, [but only if the status of the bond is "HELD"](https://www.nsw.gov.au/housing-and-construction/renting-a-place-to-live/residential-rental-bonds/rental-bonds-online-for-tenants "Rental Bonds Online for tenants") in Rental Bonds Online.

If a tenant doesn't agree with a [landlord's or agent's claim on their bond](https://www.nsw.gov.au/housing-and-construction/landlords/rental-bonds-online-for-landlords "Rental Bonds Online for self-managing landlords"), the tenant should try to talk to their landlord or agent about what could be done to deal with the dispute and try to come to an agreement.

If they cannot come to an agreement, they need to apply to the Tribunal and [notify NSW Rental Bonds](https://www.nsw.gov.au/housing-and-construction/renting-a-place-to-live/residential-rental-bonds/rental-bonds-online-for-tenants "Rental Bonds Online for tenants"), before the 'due for payment' date.

When a co-tenant moves out, they can ask the remaining co-tenants to repay their share of the rental bond. If the bond share is not repaid within 14 days, the former co-tenant may [apply to the Tribunal for an order about how the bond should be paid between the co-tenants](https://www.nsw.gov.au/housing-and-construction/rules/sharing-a-residential-rental-property#toc-claiming-the-rental-bond-at-the-end-of-a-shared-tenancy "Tribunal for an order about how the bond should be paid between the co-tenants").

If you have left your tenancy because of domestic abuse, see [Tenant protections for domestic violence and abuse in a rental property](https://www.nsw.gov.au/housing-and-construction/renting-a-place-to-live/tenant-protections-for-domestic-violence-and-abuse-a-rental-property "Tenant protections for domestic violence and abuse in a rental property") for information about getting your rental bond back.

In other cases, tenants can give 14 days’ written notice to end a fixed-term agreement early without penalty if:

*   they have accepted an offer of social housing (e.g. from DCJ Housing)
*   they need to move into an aged care facility or nursing home (not a retirement village)
*   the landlord has breached the agreement or has not disclosed something they were [required to disclose](https://www.nsw.gov.au/housing-and-construction/rules/what-tenants-need-to-be-told-about-a-rental-property "What tenants need to be told about a rental property") before entering the agreement.

Tenants can also end a fixed term agreement of 2 years or more early and without penalty if they have been given a rent increase notice. They must give 21 days’ written notice to the landlord before the rent increase starts.

Tenants need to pay the rent until they hand back possession of the property.

retrieved.section: Ending a tenancy after the landlord has given a termination notice
section_path: When break fees do not apply
Ending a tenancy after the landlord has given a termination notice
retrieved.embedding_text:
Breaking a fixed-term residential tenancy early > When break fees do not apply > Ending a tenancy after the landlord has given a termination notice
If a landlord gives a tenant in a fixed-term agreement a termination notice, the tenant has the option to leave before the end of the term without penalty. To do this they must give an early exit notice.

The early exit notice must be given to the landlord or agent.

The notice must:

*   tell the landlord that the tenant will move out before the termination date, and
*   include the date the tenant will give vacant possession of the property. 

The date for vacant possession must be at least 14 days after the notice is given to the landlord. If the tenant has fully moved out by the date given in the early exit notice, then they do not have to pay a break fee.

There are limits on when the early exit notice can be given.

*   **For fixed-term agreements of 6 months or less –**the notice can only be given in the last 60 days of the agreement.
*   **For fixed-term agreements of more than 6 months** – the notice can only be given in the last 90 days of the agreement.

If the landlord is ending the tenancy due to a breach of agreement or because the property is unusable, then the tenant cannot give an early exit notice.

[Download a sample early exit notice](https://www.nsw.gov.au/housing-and-construction/rental-forms-surveys-and-data/resources/early-exit-notice-form)

retrieved.section: Ending a tenancy after the landlord has given a termination notice
section_path: When break fees do not apply
Ending a tenancy after the landlord has given a termination notice
retrieved.embedding_text:
Breaking a fixed-term residential tenancy early > When break fees do not apply > Ending a tenancy after the landlord has given a termination notice
If a landlord gives a tenant in a fixed-term agreement a termination notice, the tenant has the option to leave before the end of the term without penalty. To do this they must give an early exit notice.

The early exit notice must be given to the landlord or agent.

The notice must:

*   tell the landlord that the tenant will move out before the termination date, and
*   include the date the tenant will give vacant possession of the property. 

The date for vacant possession must be at least 14 days after the notice is given to the landlord. If the tenant has fully moved out by the date given in the early exit notice, then they do not have to pay a break fee.

There are limits on when the early exit notice can be given.

*   **For fixed-term agreements of 6 months or less –**the notice can only be given in the last 60 days of the agreement.
*   **For fixed-term agreements of more than 6 months** – the notice can only be given in the last 90 days of the agreement.

If the landlord is ending the tenancy due to a breach of agreement or because the property is unusable, then the tenant cannot give an early exit notice.

[Download a sample early exit notice](https://www.nsw.gov.au/housing-and-construction/rental-forms-surveys-and-data/resources/early-exit-notice-form)

retrieved.section: Steps to get urgent repairs done
section_path: Steps to get urgent repairs done
retrieved.embedding_text:
Getting repairs done on a rental property > Steps to get urgent repairs done
1

Tell them – in writing if possible – about what needs fixing.

2

Follow up any conversations in writing.

3

Keep a copy of any correspondence or conversations as evidence.

4

If your landlord or agent cannot be contacted or is unwilling or taking too long to arrange repairs, check whether your lease includes details of a preferred tradesperson.

5

Get the repair work done by a licensed tradesperson, preferably one that has been recommended on your lease.

Your landlord or agent may not have to reimburse you for the cost of the repair if:

*   you [caused the damage](https://www.nsw.gov.au/housing-and-construction/rules/fair-wear-and-tear-versus-damage-rental-properties "Fair wear and tear versus damage in rental properties")
*   you didn’t try to contact them about the repair
*   you didn’t give them a reasonable amount of time to organise the repair
*   the repair was not carried out by a licensed tradesperson.

6

Make sure you send written details of repairs, including receipts for the costs, so you can get repaid.

7

You can get repaid for the cost of the work up to $1,000.Your landlord or agent must pay you back within 14 days of your notice.

retrieved.section: What if things go wrong?
section_path: What if things go wrong?
retrieved.embedding_text:
Getting repairs done on a rental property > What if things go wrong?
If urgent repairs are not done:

*   do not stop paying the rent. If you [stop paying your rent](https://www.nsw.gov.au/housing-and-construction/rules/non-payment-of-rent "Non-payment of rent"), you will be in breach of your lease agreement, and you could be asked to move out.

For urgent repairs, you need to show that:

*   the problem needing repair was not your fault
*   you made a ‘reasonable’ attempt to contact the landlord/agent
*   you allowed the landlord or agent a ‘reasonable’ chance to do the repairs
*   a repair person named in your tenancy agreement (if possible) or a licensed or qualified tradesperson did the repairs
*   you have copies of all receipts and records of conversations or letters that you have written.

You will need to have your landlord or agent's agreement if any non-urgent repairs are needed and [follow the steps outlined above](https://www.nsw.gov.au/housing-and-construction/renting-a-place-to-live/getting-repairs-done#non-urgent-repairs)to get them done.

If a repair issue is not able to be resolved, you can [lodge a complaint to NSW Fair Trading](https://www.nsw.gov.au/housing-and-construction/renting-a-place-to-live/residential-tenancy-complaints "Residential tenancy complaints") to get help. If the landlord or agent doesn't want to carry out the repairs, NSW Fair Trading may decide to issue a [rectification order](https://www.nsw.gov.au/housing-and-construction/rules/rectification-orders-for-rental-properties "Rectification orders for rental properties").

If this still does not solve the issue, you can escalate the [dispute to the Tribunal](https://www.nsw.gov.au/housing-and-construction/renting-a-place-to-live/residential-rental-bonds/dealing-bond-disputes-for-tenants#toc-going-to-the-tribunal)(NSW Civil and Administrative Tribunal (NCAT)).

To get help and support, go to the [Tenants’ Union of NSW](https://www.tenants.org.au/ "Tenants' Union of New South Wales (https://www.tenants.org.au/)") for legal advice, assistance, and information to tenants, with resources in community languages available. The[NSW Aboriginal Tenancy Advice and Advocacy Services](https://nswats.com.au/how-we-help/) also offers assistance and support for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander tenants.

Request advice before a Tribunal hearing

Do you have a date for a hearing in the NSW Civil and Administrative Tribunal (NCAT)? Get advice from your local Tenants Advice and Advocacy Service.

[Use the Tenants' Union request form](https://www.tenants.org.au/ncatadvice).

section_path: How do I request a repair be made?
retrieved.embedding_text:
Getting repairs done on a rental property > How do I request a repair be made?
There are two types of repairs: [urgent repairs](https://www.nsw.gov.au/housing-and-construction/renting-a-place-to-live/getting-repairs-done#urgent-repairs) and [non-urgent repairs](https://www.nsw.gov.au/housing-and-construction/renting-a-place-to-live/getting-repairs-done#non-urgent-repairs).

In both circumstances you should contact your landlord or real estate agent first.

If you require urgent repairs and you can't contact your landlord or agent, then you can contact a repair person yourself - see your [residential tenancy agreement](https://www.nsw.gov.au/housing-and-construction/rules/residential-tenancy-agreements "Residential tenancy agreements") for approved or preferred tradespeople to use - and have the costs reimbursed up to $1,000.

retrieved.section: Resolving disputes through the Tribunal
section_path: Resolving disputes through the Tribunal
retrieved.embedding_text:
Resolving residential tenancy disputes > Resolving disputes through the Tribunal
The Tribunal is an independent body that hears and decides on applications for orders from tenants and landlords.

A landlord or tenant can apply directly to the Tribunal for orders relating to a residential tenancy instead of first [making a complaint to Fair Trading](https://www.nsw.gov.au/housing-and-construction/renting-a-place-to-live/residential-tenancy-complaints "Tenancy complaints"), if they wish.

A landlord or tenant can decide to lodge an application with the Tribunal if:

*   Fair Trading cannot find a solution mutually agreed to by both parties.
*   A termination order is being sought.
*   The complaint relates to a matter for which Fair Trading is not able to offer dispute resolution, such as a dispute relating to claiming a bond.

section_path: Repairs, maintenance or damage disputes
retrieved.embedding_text:
Resolving residential tenancy disputes > Repairs, maintenance or damage disputes
If a tenant or landlord is unable to resolve a dispute about repairs, maintenance or damage through [NSW Fair Trading's tenancy and real estate complaint service](https://www.nsw.gov.au/housing-and-construction/renting-a-place-to-live/residential-tenancy-complaints "Residential tenancy complaints"), either party may be able to have the dispute investigated further.

Fair Trading can investigate whether:

*   the landlord has breached their obligation to provide and maintain the property in a reasonable state of repair.
*   the tenant has caused (or permitted) damage to the property and failed to satisfactorily repair the damage without a reasonable excuse.

Fair Trading will then decide whether to issue a [landlord or tenant rectification order](https://www.nsw.gov.au/housing-and-construction/rules/rectification-orders-for-rental-properties "Rectification orders for rental properties") based on these investigations.

The NSW Civil and Administrative Tribunal (the Tribunal) can also make orders relating to repairs, maintenance or damage to the property.

A tenant is not responsible for property damage caused by domestic abuse if they are not the alleged perpetrator of the domestic abuse.

If there is a dispute about whether the damage was caused by domestic abuse, the Tribunal must consider evidence of domestic abuse and make an assessment on the civil standard of proof, known as the balance of probabilities. See [Tenant protections for domestic violence and abuse in a rental property](https://www.nsw.gov.au/housing-and-construction/renting-a-place-to-live/tenant-protections-for-domestic-violence-and-abuse-a-rental-property "Tenant protections for domestic violence and abuse in a rental property") for more information.

section_path: How do I request a repair be made?
retrieved.embedding_text:
Getting repairs done on a rental property > How do I request a repair be made?
There are two types of repairs: [urgent repairs](https://www.nsw.gov.au/housing-and-construction/renting-a-place-to-live/getting-repairs-done#urgent-repairs) and [non-urgent repairs](https://www.nsw.gov.au/housing-and-construction/renting-a-place-to-live/getting-repairs-done#non-urgent-repairs).

In both circumstances you should contact your landlord or real estate agent first.

If you require urgent repairs and you can't contact your landlord or agent, then you can contact a repair person yourself - see your [residential tenancy agreement](https://www.nsw.gov.au/housing-and-construction/rules/residential-tenancy-agreements "Residential tenancy agreements") for approved or preferred tradespeople to use - and have the costs reimbursed up to $1,000.

What if things go wrong?
retrieved.embedding_text:
Getting your bond back at the end of a tenancy > Getting your bond back at the end of a tenancy > What if things go wrong?
Things may go wrong if

*   you have not addressed all the things you need to do when ending a tenancy
*   you have a disagreement with your landlord or agent and need to negotiate
*   your [landlord or agent disputes your claim](https://www.nsw.gov.au/housing-and-construction/renting-a-place-to-live/residential-rental-bonds/dealing-bond-disputes-for-tenants "Dealing with bond disputes for tenants")
*   you cannot afford to pay for [damages beyond fair wear and tear](https://www.nsw.gov.au/housing-and-construction/rules/fair-wear-and-tear-versus-damage-rental-properties "Fair wear and tear versus damage in rental properties").

If the issue is not able to be resolved, you or your landlord or agent may need to[take the dispute to the NSW Civil and Administrative Tribunal (NCAT)](https://ncat.nsw.gov.au/case-types/housing-and-property.html "NSW Civil and Administrative Tribunal (https://ncat.nsw.gov.au/case-types/housing-and-property.html)"). This means that the dispute is out of Fair Trading NSW's hands.

To get help, go to the [Tenants’ Union of NSW](https://www.tenants.org.au/ "Tenants' Union of New South Wales (https://www.tenants.org.au/)") for legal advice, assistance, and information to tenants. The Tribunal also provides a useful [list of links to legal help and advice services](https://ncat.nsw.gov.au/help-and-support/get-legal-help-and-advice.html).

If your tenancy is over, you can claim the bond back online

You don’t need to wait for the landlord to release the bond. If you originally submitted your bond online and you have addressed all the things you need to do after ending the tenancy, you can claim the bond on Rental Bonds Online.

[Claim the bond online](https://rbo.fairtrading.nsw.gov.au/tenant/login "Rental Bonds Online registered tenant login (https://rbo.fairtrading.nsw.gov.au/tenant/login)")

Make a complaint to NSW Fair Trading about a bond claim without evidence

If your agent or landlord makes a claim against the bond and does not provide you with evidence of the claim, this is a breach of the Residential Tenancies Act 2010. You should lodge a complaint with NSW Fair Trading to assess their conduct.

[Lodge a complaint with Fair Trading](https://www.nsw.gov.au/housing-and-construction/renting-a-place-to-live/residential-tenancy-complaints "Residential tenancy complaints").

Request advice before a Tribunal hearing

Do you have a date for a hearing in the NSW Civil and Administrative Tribunal (NCAT)? Get advice from your local Tenants Advice and Advocacy Service.

[Use the Tenants' Union request form](https://www.tenants.org.au/ncatadvice)

* * *
